metric.why: Rates rising after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply. Rate data is compiled by commercial research firms listed in the directory below; it is not republished here.
metric.definition: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.

reading.body:
After a decade of declining rates, colocation rental prices are rising in major metros, the clearest market signal that AI compute demand has outpaced available supply.

When capacity exceeds demand, prices fall. When demand exceeds capacity, prices rise. The reversal of a ten-year downward trend in colocation rates indicates the market has shifted. Colocation facilities lease power and floor space to customers who bring their own equipment, making the rental rate per kilowatt a direct measure of how scarce that combination has become. Rising rates mean customers now bid against each other for limited slots.

This matters for AI because hyperscalers and smaller operators alike depend on colocation to expand capacity quickly. When rates climb, it costs more to scale. The data does not isolate AI demand from other workloads, nor does it show whether prices are rising because new capacity is being built too slowly or because AI adoption is accelerating faster than expected. It does not track whether builders are responding to higher rates by constructing new facilities. But the direction is unambiguous: the market believes power and floor space are now harder to get than they were.
